newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt softening towards cotton liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: Egypt softening towards cotton liberalisation.

text.p: Egypt appears to be softening its stand on liberalisation of the lucrative cotton market and may soon end its de facto monopoly on the crop by subsidising private sector traders, officials and traders say.

Public Administration Minister Atef Obeid told a meeting of private and public sector cotton traders on Sunday the state was studying a proposal to pay the difference between export prices and the higher minimum price paid to farmers, in order to let private traders back into the market.
The floor price of 500 pounds ($147) per qantar (50 kg) was first set in the 1995/1996 season to encourage farmers to cultivate cotton for export.
The minimum price -- higher than international levels -- sidelined private sector traders and almost all raw cotton was scooped up by state firms, which already benefit from government subsidies.
"If taken, this decision will increase exports tremendously and if we use logic it will be done soon," said Amin Abaza, managing director of the private Modern Nile Cotton Company.
"I'm convinced that it is the only solution and if the government wants to subsidise them (farmers) then it should do that without affecting the market equilibrium," he told Reuters.
According to the Alexandria Cotton Exporters Association (Alcotexa), private firms are committed to export only 4,305 tonnes out of total commitments of 62,688 tonnes so far this season.

The government has said it wants to export up to 150,000 tonnes of this season's 350,000-tonne bumper harvest. This year Egypt said it would increase by 100,000 acres to one million acres the area planted with cotton and forecast this area would yield 400,000 tonnes of cotton.
"We want a bigger role. We can't buy seed cotton because of the state monopoly and we're going out of business in the internal market," said Medhat el-Alfi of Nassco Trading.

"We want to be able to buy the cotton with competitive prices straight from the farmer, gin it and sell it ourselves. If the government wants to keep these subisidies, it should support us," he added.

Obeid, who calls himself the state's salesman and is responsible for Egypt's privatisation programme which is the flagship of its economic reforms, said he hoped the proposal would boost exports of the cash crop by 300 percent.
But traders said the ministries of finance, agriculture and parliament must approve the proposal before privatisation spreads to the cotton sector.
Saeed Haggag, head of Alcotexa which coordinates export prices of private and public sector firms, called the minimum price a "calamity" motivated by politics and not economics.

"The government puts an attractive minimum price so that farmers don't plant the more lucrative fodder. We put the export prices to compete with international markets. The difference amounts to hundreds of millions each season," he said.

According to Agriculture Ministry Undersecretary Zeinhom Farag, the state paid 720 million pounds in subsidies this season but he defended the state's position because of the "strategic nature" of the crop.

"We tried two seasons ago to get out of the market but the harvest was small and there was manipulation and hoarding by the private firms. We also need to have control over the cotton hybrids so the most saleable can be planted," he said.
Farag and other Egyptian officials said the state was considering setting up a fund to finance the cotton trade but they have not yet found backers for the project.
